sections.SI: Structural Integrity Indicators (3 indicators - Critical Stage 1)
sections.PIC: Pedagogical Integrity Indicators - Core (5 indicators - High Priority Stage 2)
sections.PIA: Pedagogical Integrity Indicators - Advanced (5 indicators - Developmental Stage 3+)
sections.MA: Model Alignment Indicators (1 indicator - Optimization Stage 4)

SI1.name: Instructional Clarity
SI1.description: The teacher clearly communicates the lesson's purpose and learning expectations — stating goals explicitly and explaining content in a logical, coherent sequence. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether the teacher states a clear learning goal early in the lesson and whether explanations follow a logical structure with connectors — making content easy to follow.

YES: States "Today we will learn [specific skill/concept]" within first 5 minutes
Uses precise academic vocabulary (defines terms before using them)
Explanations follow logical sequence with connectors ("first," "next," "because," "therefore")
Checks for understanding of instructions: "Does everyone understand what to do?"
PARTIAL: Goal mentioned but vague ("We're learning about animals" vs. "classify animals by characteristics")
OR explanations use 1-2 logical connectors but lack full coherence
OR teacher checks understanding only at end, not during explanations
NO: No explicit goal statement in first 10 minutes
Explanations jump between ideas without connectors
Vague language: "You know," "this thing," "kind of like"
No comprehension checks

SI1.aiDetectionMethod: Scan first 5 minutes for phrases: "Today we will," "By the end," "You will learn". Count logical connectors (first, next, because, therefore, so, then). Identify comprehension check questions. Analyze vocabulary precision vs. vague language frequency.
SI1.rationale: All evidence is purely verbal - goal statements, logical connectors, and comprehension checks are spoken aloud. AI can detect key phrases, count logical connectors, identify vague vs. precise language, and timestamp when goals are stated. No visual information required.

SI2.name: Logical Flow
SI2.description: The lesson progresses coherently from opening through instruction to closure. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether the lesson has three identifiable phases — beginning, middle, and end — with logical topic coherence throughout.

YES: Clear opening: Introduction of topic/objective within first 5 minutes
Distinct middle section: Core instruction and activities
Clear closure: Wrap-up or summary at lesson end
Transition signals connect segments: "Now that we've..., let's move to...", "Next, we will..."
Verbal markers indicate progression: "First," "Next," "Now," "Finally," "To conclude"
Logical topic coherence throughout (doesn't jump randomly)
PARTIAL: Basic structure present but transitions are abrupt or unclear
Missing clear opening OR closure (but has 2 out of 3 phases)
Some transition language but inconsistent (1-2 markers only)
Minor topic jumping but generally coherent
NO: Disjointed lesson flow with no clear beginning, middle, or end
No transition signals between activities
Jumps randomly between topics without connectors
Lesson feels like disconnected segments

SI2.aiDetectionMethod: Identify temporal phase markers in first 5 minutes (beginning indicators: "today we will," "let's start with," "first"). Identify middle phase markers (instruction/activity language). Identify closure markers (end indicators: "to conclude," "in summary," "let's review," "finally"). Count sequential connectors. Detect transition signals. Analyze topic coherence. Track lesson timeline.
SI2.rationale: Teacher uses verbal markers to signal lesson structure and transitions. AI can identify phase markers with timestamps, count sequential connectors, detect transition signals, analyze topic coherence, track distinct phases, and distinguish between smooth transitions vs. abrupt segment changes. No visual information required.

SI3.name: Subject Content Accuracy
SI3.description: The teacher delivers factually correct content, accurate definitions, and clear explanations throughout the lesson. WHAT TO MEASURE: Correctness of facts, definitions, and explanations — distinguishing minor non-critical slips from significant errors that mislead learning.

YES: All facts stated are conceptually correct
Definitions accurate and complete
Responses to student questions are correct and clear
No misconceptions reinforced
May include 0–1 minor non-critical slip (e.g., pronunciation, wording, small detail)
PARTIAL: Content is mostly accurate
1–2 minor errors that have minimal impact on learning (e.g., pronunciation, small factual detail, wording)
Teacher may show uncertainty language (e.g., "I think…", "I'm not sure but…")
Core concept is still correctly explained
NO: Significant factual errors that mislead learning
Incorrect definitions or explanations
Statements that conflict with established facts
Reinforces misconceptions

SI3.aiDetectionMethod: Fact extraction and verification against knowledge base. Definition comparison to standard sources. Uncertainty language detection: "I think," "maybe," "not sure". Identification of conceptual inaccuracies or misconceptions.
SI3.rationale: All factual content, definitions, and explanations are spoken aloud. AI can extract facts and verify against knowledge base, compare definitions to standard sources, detect uncertainty language, identify misconceptions in teacher explanations, and track correctness of responses to student questions. No visual information required.

PIC-1.name: Activities & Tasks Alignment
PIC-1.description: The teacher's activities, tasks, and questions are connected to the learning objective and match its cognitive level (remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, creating). WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether activities align with the stated SLO AND match the cognitive level intended in the objective.

YES: Activities and tasks clearly connected to the stated SLO
Activities match the cognitive level of the SLO (e.g., analysis tasks for analysis-level objectives)
Questions asked during lesson match the cognitive demand of the objective
PARTIAL: Activities connected to SLO BUT cognitive level doesn't match — SLO requires analysis but activities are recall only
OR some activities match cognitive level but others don't
OR activities seem relevant but connection to SLO is unclear
NO: Activities appear random and disconnected from stated objective
Cognitive level completely mismatched — SLO requires higher-order thinking but all tasks are pure recall

PIC-1.aiDetectionMethod: Match activity and task keywords to SLO keywords. Extract and classify task verbs (using Bloom's taxonomy). Compare cognitive level of tasks to cognitive level stated in SLO. Assess whether activities conducted relate to stated learning objective.
PIC-1.rationale: All evidence is verbalized by teacher - explicit connections between activities and objectives, plus verbal explanation of cognitive level. Activity content and cognitive level are detectable through task instructions and question types in transcript. Bloom's taxonomy classification of task verbs is achievable through NLP. No visual information required.

PIC-2.name: Use of Academic Language
PIC-2.description: The teacher uses subject-specific terminology correctly and models it for students. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether technical terms are used accurately, defined when first introduced, and modeled consistently throughout the lesson.

YES: Uses technical terms correctly: "photosynthesis," "denominator," "habitat"
Defines terms when first used: "A habitat is where an animal lives"
Models proper usage: "We call this a rectangle because..."
Corrects student language: "We say 'sum' not 'answer' in addition"
PARTIAL: Uses some technical terms but inconsistently
Terms used but not defined
NO: Avoids technical vocabulary
Uses incorrect terminology
Casual language throughout: "thingy," "stuff," "that part"

PIC-2.aiDetectionMethod: Identify subject-specific vocabulary from glossary. Count academic term frequency. Detect definition patterns: "is," "means," "called". Track vague language frequency.
PIC-2.rationale: Teacher verbalizes technical terminology and definitions. AI can identify subject-specific vocabulary from glossary, count academic term frequency (target: 5+ terms), detect definition patterns, track if terms are defined when first introduced, monitor corrections to student language, and compare vague vs. precise language frequency. No visual information required.

PIC-3.name: Understanding Student Misconceptions
PIC-3.description: The teacher identifies and accurately corrects student errors and misconceptions during the lesson. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether the teacher recognizes incorrect student responses and corrects them accurately — not just acknowledges them.

YES: Identifies incorrect student response and corrects it accurately
Addresses common misconceptions proactively: "Many people think X, but actually..."
Prevents reinforcement of errors — does not accept wrong answers as correct
PARTIAL: Recognizes error but correction is incomplete or inaccurate
Says "wrong" but does not provide correct answer
NO: Accepts incorrect student answers without correction
Reinforces misconceptions: "Yes, that's right" when answer is wrong
Provides incorrect corrections

PIC-3.aiDetectionMethod: Detect correction patterns: "not quite," "actually," "that's incorrect," "the correct answer is". Identify proactive misconception language: "many people think". Track incorrect student responses followed by teacher correction. Verify correction accuracy against knowledge base. Distinguish accurate corrections from incomplete or wrong ones.
PIC-3.rationale: Teacher verbalizes corrections and addresses misconceptions through dialogue. AI can detect correction patterns, identify proactive misconception language, track incorrect student responses followed by teacher response, count misconceptions identified and addressed (target: 2+), and distinguish complete corrections from incomplete ones. No visual information required.

PIC-4.name: Quality Questioning
PIC-4.description: The teacher asks open-ended questions to promote thinking and uses probing follow-ups to deepen student responses. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether the teacher initiates critical thinking through open-ended questions AND deepens it through probing follow-ups.

YES: Asks open-ended questions requiring reasoning: "Why," "How," "What if," "Explain"
Does not accept surface answers — probes deeper: "Why do you think that?" "Can you explain more?" "How do you know?"
Pushes for justification after student responses
PARTIAL: Asks open-ended questions but does not probe deeper — accepts first answer and moves on
OR probes occasionally but majority of questions are closed or recall-based
NO: Predominantly yes/no or recall questions throughout
No probing follow-ups at any point
Students never pushed beyond one-word or surface answers

PIC-4.aiDetectionMethod: Classify all questions (open vs. closed). Calculate % open-ended. Identify probing sequences — student answer followed by teacher follow-up question. Count "why," "how," "explain," "justify" after student responses. Track open questions + probing follow-ups separately.
PIC-4.rationale: All questions are spoken aloud - both initial and follow-up probing. AI can classify all questions (open vs. closed), calculate percentage open-ended (target: 70%+), identify probing sequences (student answer → teacher follow-up), count "why," "how," "explain" after student responses, and track minimum 5 open questions + 3 probing follow-ups. No visual information required.

PIC-5.name: Effective Feedback
PIC-5.description: The teacher provides specific, actionable verbal feedback that helps students understand what is correct, what is incorrect, and how to improve. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether verbal feedback is specific and actionable — going beyond generic praise or correction to guide student improvement.

YES: Feedback is specific and directly related to the task or learning objective
Describes what is correct or incorrect: "You added instead of multiplied in step 3"
Affirms with detail: "Your answer is correct because you identified the main idea"
Guides next steps: "Try using this formula..." / "Next time, start by..."
Feedback goes beyond generic praise or correction — students know what to do differently
PARTIAL: Feedback present but generic throughout: "Good job," "Wrong," "Try again" — no explanation or guidance
OR feedback is specific occasionally but inconsistent — some responses get quality feedback, others ignored
OR feedback acknowledges response but does not guide improvement
NO: No meaningful feedback given after student responses
OR all feedback is generic with no guidance whatsoever
OR feedback is so delayed it is disconnected from the student's response

PIC-5.aiDetectionMethod: Identify student response moments in transcript. Check if teacher feedback follows within same exchange. Classify feedback as generic (praise/correction only) vs. specific (error description + guidance). Identify guidance language: "try," "use," "add," "change," "next time," "instead," "because". Detect affirmation with detail vs. empty praise.
PIC-5.rationale: Feedback is spoken immediately after student responses. AI can timestamp student responses and teacher feedback, calculate time gaps (target: within 5 seconds), classify feedback (generic vs. specific), identify guidance language ("try," "use," "add," "change"), and track feedback rate (target: 80%+ responses get immediate feedback). No visual information required.

PIA-1.name: Prior Knowledge
PIA-1.description: The teacher activates students' existing knowledge and builds on their responses to connect to new content. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether the teacher elicits prior knowledge AND genuinely builds on student responses — both must be present.

YES: Teacher actively elicits what students already know — through questions, prompts, or references to past learning
Teacher genuinely builds on student responses — uses what students say to bridge into new content
PARTIAL: Asks about prior knowledge but doesn't wait for or build on responses
OR makes connections to past learning without checking what students actually remember
NO: Lesson starts directly with new content
No mention of previous learning at any point
Teacher doesn't ask what students remember

PIA-1.aiDetectionMethod: Search for recall prompts: "remember," "last time," "we learned," "what do you know about". Detect question-response-building sequences. Identify temporal references to past lessons. Track whether teacher uses student responses to bridge into new content.
PIA-1.rationale: Teacher explicitly verbalizes connections to prior learning and student responses are audible. Prior knowledge elicitation and building are entirely verbal — spoken dialogue fully capturable in transcript. AI can detect recall questions and temporal references through pattern analysis. Question-response-building sequences detectable through dialogue structure analysis. No visual information required.

PIA-2.name: Meaningful Connections
PIA-2.description: The teacher connects new content to something students can relate to — through real life examples, analogies, or cross-curricular links. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether connections are explicitly verbalized and clearly explained — not just briefly mentioned.

YES: Provides concrete real life examples: "Like when you [familiar experience]..."
Uses analogies: "Think of this as similar to..."
Real-world applications: "You use this when you [daily activity]..."
Cross-curricular connections: "Remember in science when we..."
Connection is clearly explained — not just mentioned
PARTIAL: Mentions connections but doesn't fully explain them
Examples are superficial: "This is like real life" (without specifics)
Connection mentioned but not elaborated enough for students to understand how it relates
NO: Purely abstract teaching
No examples, analogies, or applications provided
Content taught entirely in isolation with nothing relatable

PIA-2.aiDetectionMethod: Search for connection phrases: "like when," "for example," "imagine," "in real life," "similar to," "remember in". Identify analogy structures: "X is like Y because...". Detect cross-curricular references: subject names, previous topic references. Distinguish elaborated connections from superficial mentions. Count distinct connection instances.
PIA-2.rationale: Teacher verbalizes examples, analogies, and applications to make content relatable. AI can detect connection phrases, identify analogy structures, count distinct examples/connections (target: 3+), distinguish detailed explanations from superficial mentions, and analyze depth of examples provided. No visual information required.

MA-0.name: Instructional Model Structure
MA-0.description: The lesson follows a structured instructional model with a clear gradual release of responsibility — moving from teacher-led to student-led work. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether all three instructional phases are present — teacher modeling (I Do), guided practice (We Do), and independent practice (You Do) — with teacher support visibly decreasing across the lesson.

YES: Teacher modeling: Teacher demonstrates or explains the new concept/skill
Guided practice: Teacher and students work together with teacher providing support
Independent practice: Students work on their own with minimal teacher intervention
Key evidence: Teacher support and involvement decreases as lesson progresses (from high support to low support)
PARTIAL: Two phases present but missing one (commonly skips guided practice, jumping from modeling directly to independent work)
OR all three phases present but teacher support level remains constant (no gradual release evident)
OR one phase very brief or unclear
NO: Lesson dominated by single mode: all lecture OR all independent work
No evidence of instructional progression
Missing two or more phases

MA-0.aiDetectionMethod: Track teacher talk ratio across lesson timeline. Identify three phases: teacher modeling (high teacher talk), collaborative work (mixed voices), independent work (low teacher talk). Verify teacher talk decreases over time (e.g., 80% to 50% to 20%). Detect phase transitions through changes in interaction patterns.
MA-0.rationale: Gradual Release of Responsibility is audio-detectable through teacher-student talk patterns. AI can measure teacher talk percentage over time and identify when instruction shifts from teacher-led to student-led. Critical distinction: measures instructional model (I Do/We Do/You Do), not just lesson structure. No visual information required.

M1.name: Mathematical Discourse & Reasoning
M1.description: The teacher pushes students to explain their mathematical thinking and justify their solutions — focusing on process, not just the answer. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether the teacher asks students to explain HOW they solved a problem and whether students produce audible mathematical reasoning at a level appropriate to their grade.

YES: Teacher asks reasoning questions: "How do you know?" / "Why does that work?" / "Tell me how you solved it"

Students produce audible mathematical reasoning — any level accepted: Grade 1-2: "I counted on my fingers" / "because 2 and 2 make 4"; Grade 3-5: "I first added then subtracted" / "I knew it was wrong because..."
Teacher presses for reasoning — does not accept answer-only responses
PARTIAL: Teacher asks reasoning questions but accepts one-word or answer-only responses without pressing further
OR reasoning prompted but students never produce explanation — teacher moves on
NO: Entirely answer-focused throughout: "What is the answer?" with no how or why
No student mathematical explanation at any point

M1.aiDetectionMethod: Count reasoning questions: "how," "why," "explain," "justify," "show me". Detect student explanation patterns — sentence-level mathematical reasoning. Distinguish process-focused vs. answer-focused questions. Track whether teacher presses after student response or accepts answer only.
M1.rationale: Teacher and students engage in verbal mathematical reasoning - questions about thinking and audible student explanations. AI can count reasoning questions, detect student explanation patterns in dialogue, measure wait time after questions, distinguish process-focused vs. answer-focused questions, and track multiple student explanations (target: 5+ reasoning questions). No visual information required.

M2.name: Problem-Solving & Productive Struggle
M2.description: The teacher presents challenging problems and allows students adequate think time to struggle productively — without rushing in with answers. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether a genuinely challenging problem is presented, sufficient think time is allowed, and the teacher encourages persistence rather than immediately providing solutions.

YES: Teacher presents a problem that requires genuine thinking — not routine procedural practice: Multi-step, non-routine, or unfamiliar problem type
Teacher allows adequate think time appropriate to the problem — does not rush or immediately provide the answer when students struggle
Encourages persistence: "Keep trying, you're on the right track"
Doesn't immediately give answers when students struggle
PARTIAL: Problem is presented but think time is too brief — teacher moves on or gives the answer before students have meaningfully engaged
OR problem is challenging but teacher's stance undermines struggle — jumps in too quickly, gives hints that remove the challenge
OR encouragement is present but no real think time is given
NO: Only routine procedural practice (no problem-solving)
Teacher immediately provides solutions
No think time allowed

M2.aiDetectionMethod: Identify problem complexity (multi-step, non-routine). Measure silent think time duration. Detect encouragement language during difficulty.
M2.rationale: Teacher verbalizes problem presentation, think time instructions, and encouragement. AI can identify problem complexity through language (multi-step, non-routine), measure silent think time duration, detect encouragement language during difficulty ("Keep trying," "You're on the right track"), track if teacher provides immediate answers vs. allowing struggle, and timestamp think time (target: 2+ minutes). No visual information required.

S1.name: Inquiry-Based Approach
S1.description: The teacher structures concept introduction so students think first — rather than being told the answer immediately. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether the teacher withholds the answer and creates genuine space for student thinking before explaining — at any point in the lesson.

YES: When introducing or exploring a concept, teacher does NOT give answer first
Opens concept with a question, picture, or scenario at any point in lesson
Students are given genuine space to respond before teacher explains
Teacher builds on at least one student response to guide toward concept
PARTIAL: Teacher attempts inquiry opening but gives answer too quickly
OR starts with inquiry but shifts to pure transmission and never returns
OR asks "what do you think?" but dismisses all responses and explains anyway
NO: Teacher starts directly with definition or explanation
No space for student thinking at any point
Pure transmission throughout

S1.aiDetectionMethod: Detect inquiry moments at any point — not just lesson opening. Track sequence — does student thinking come BEFORE teacher explanation each time? Identify teacher prompts: "what do you think," "what do you notice," "what would happen if". Detect whether teacher builds on at least one student response.
S1.rationale: Inquiry sequence is entirely verbal and detectable through transcript timing analysis. Whether teacher gives answer first OR asks students to think first is clearly detectable in audio. No visual information required — inquiry structure communicated entirely through spoken dialogue.

S2.name: Science Talk & Student Sense-Making
S2.description: Students express science ideas in their own words — rather than echoing the teacher or giving one-word answers. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether students verbally make sense of science concepts in their own words — student talk quality only, not teacher behavior.

YES: Students express science ideas in their own words — not repeating teacher's exact phrase
At least 2 students produce sentence-level science responses — not one-word or chorus answers
Students use any form of reasoning: "I think because..." / "Maybe it's because..."
PARTIAL: Some sentence-level responses but majority are one-word or chorus answers
Students express ideas but only by repeating teacher's exact wording
Only 1 student produces own-words expression
NO: All student responses are one-word, chorus, or direct repetition of teacher's words
No student expresses a science idea in their own words at any point
Pure IRE throughout — teacher asks, student gives one word, teacher moves on

S2.aiDetectionMethod: Measure student talk length — one-word vs. sentence-level science expression. Detect student-generated language — own words vs. repeating teacher. Identify reasoning language in student responses: "I think," "because," "maybe," "it could be". Count students producing sentence-level science responses.
S2.rationale: Science talk is entirely verbal — all evidence captured in audio transcript. IRE vs dialogic pattern detectable through conversation analysis — teacher uptake after student response is key signal. Student talk length and content measurable through NLP — one word vs. sentence-level science expression. Teacher uptake language detectable: "building on," "yes and," "who agrees". No visual information required.

L1.name: Explicit Phonics/Decoding
L1.description: The teacher provides structured phonics instruction following a clear pedagogical sequence — from pronunciation and sound identification through to blending and segmenting. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether phonics instruction follows the correct sequence — pronunciation → initial/final sounds → blending → segmenting — not just whether phonics activities are present.

YES: Phonics instruction follows clear sequence: pronunciation → initial/final sounds → blending → segmenting
Each step explicitly taught and modeled: "/b/ is the sound for letter B" / "Listen: /c/ /a/ /t/ = cat"
Students practice at each stage — audible student responses present
Sequence is complete and consistent — no major steps skipped
PARTIAL: General phonics sequence present but inconsistencies or omissions evident
Teacher exhibits overall structure but skips or rushes through one or more steps
Some student practice present but not at every stage
NO: Phonetic drill and sequenced structure completely skipped
No phonics instruction at any point
Letters or sounds mentioned but no explicit teaching of correspondence or sequence

L1.aiDetectionMethod: Identify pronunciation modeling: teacher isolating and modeling individual sounds. Detect initial/final sound instruction: "what sound does this start with," "ending sound". Detect blending language: "/c/ /a/ /t/ = cat," "put the sounds together". Detect segmenting practice: "clap the sounds," "break the word". Track sequence — are stages appearing in correct order? Monitor student audible responses at each stage.
L1.rationale: Phonics instruction is entirely auditory — sound-letter correspondences and blending are spoken. Sequence detection possible through NLP — each stage has distinct language patterns. Student practice audible — clapping, repeating sounds, blending responses all capturable in audio. No visual information required - phonics is fundamentally about sounds and oral practice.

L2.name: Comprehension Strategy Instruction
L2.description: The teacher explicitly teaches a reading comprehension strategy by naming it, modeling it, and having students practice it. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether the complete strategy instruction sequence is present — name it, model it, practice it — all three must be present.

YES: Names the strategy explicitly: "This is called predicting" / "Today we will practice summarizing"
Models strategy with text: "Watch me – I think the next part will be about... because I can see..."
Students practice strategy audibly — attempt strategy with teacher guidance
PARTIAL: Names and models strategy but no student practice
OR students practice but strategy never explicitly named or modeled
NO: No strategy instruction at any point
Teacher asks comprehension questions but never teaches HOW to comprehend

L2.aiDetectionMethod: Identify strategy names: "predict," "infer," "visualize," "summarize," "connect". Detect modeling language: "watch me," "I think," "I'm going to". Track student practice — audible student strategy attempts. Verify all 3 steps present in sequence.
L2.rationale: Strategy instruction is entirely verbal — naming, modeling, and practice all spoken aloud. Strategy names and modeling language detectable through NLP. Student practice audible — thinking aloud, responding with predictions or inferences. No visual information required - comprehension strategies are taught and practiced through spoken thinking.

L3.name: Reading-Writing Connections
L3.description: The teacher explicitly connects reading and writing activities — using text as a model or prompt for student writing. WHAT TO MEASURE: Whether explicit verbal links between reading and writing are present — not just whether both activities happen in the same lesson.

YES: Explicit links: "We read about X, now write about..."
Uses text as model: "Notice how the author..., you can do that in your writing"
Writing in response to text: "Write what you think will happen next"
Clear connection verbalized
PARTIAL: Reading and writing both happen but connection not explicit
OR weak connection: "We read, now write" (no clear link)
NO: Reading and writing are completely separate
OR only reading OR only writing (not both)
No connection verbalized

L3.aiDetectionMethod: Search for "we read," "the author," "now write," "like in the text". Identify reading-writing bridge language.
L3.rationale: Teacher explicitly verbalizes connections between reading and writing activities. AI can search for bridge language ("we read," "the author," "now write," "like in the text"), identify reading-writing connection phrases, count explicit connections (target: 2+), distinguish explicit vs. implicit connections, and track text-as-model language ("Notice how the author..."). No visual information required.

SLGP-1.name: Diversity of Conceptual Expression
SLGP-1.description: Do students express the concept in varied ways — or do they all repeat the teacher's exact words?

YES: Students use at least 3 different phrasings of the concept
At least one student uses a word or example the teacher never introduced
Variety in student responses shows diverse thinking beyond echo-repetition
PARTIAL: Students phrase the concept in 2 or more ways but only use teacher's words
Some variety in responses but no new vocabulary or examples
Mix of diverse and echo responses
NO: All student responses copy the teacher's wording closely
Students only give very short answers (one word, number, or chorus)
No student responses about the concept present

SLGP-1.aiDetectionMethod: Extract student responses about the concept throughout the lesson. Analyze unique phrasings and new vocabulary introduced by students. Compare student language to teacher language. Identify echo-responses vs. novel expressions.

SLGP-2.name: Student Reasoning in Responses
SLGP-2.description: Do students explain why an answer is correct — not just what the answer is?

YES: At least two student responses contain an explanation or reason
At least one explanation was not prompted by teacher asking 'why'
Students demonstrate spontaneous reasoning about their answers
PARTIAL: At least one student response contains reasoning but only after teacher asked
Reasoning present but only teacher-prompted
Limited reasoning from students despite invitations
NO: Teacher asked for reasoning but no student reasoning followed
Teacher never asked for reasoning and none appears in lesson
No reasoning activity present in lesson at all

SLGP-2.aiDetectionMethod: Identify teacher prompts for reasoning ('Why', 'How do you know', 'Explain your thinking'). Extract student responses that contain because/because/reason language. Distinguish between prompted and unprompted reasoning. Count reasoning instances.

SLGP-3.name: Student-Initiated Questions
SLGP-3.description: Do any students ask a genuine content question — showing they have processed the concept enough to identify a gap or an extension?

YES: At least one student asks a genuine content question about the concept
Question goes beyond what was taught OR seeks clarification of concept
Question shows conceptual engagement, not just logistics
PARTIAL: Students ask only procedural questions without content questions
Questions are logistical: 'what page?', 'do we write it down?'
Minimal genuine curiosity about the concept demonstrated
NO: No student questions of any kind appear in the lesson
All questioning comes from teacher only
No evidence of student curiosity or clarification-seeking

SLGP-3.aiDetectionMethod: Identify student-initiated utterances that end in question mark. Classify as procedural (logistical questions) vs. content (concept-related). Verify student ownership (not teacher putting words in student's mouth). Count content questions initiated by students.

SLGP-4.name: Spontaneous Transfer and Connection-Making
SLGP-4.description: Does any student connect the lesson concept to something outside the lesson — from their own life, a previous lesson, or another subject?

YES: At least one student makes an unprompted connection to outside the lesson
Connection links concept to student's own life, previous lesson, or another subject
Transfer is spontaneous, not prompted by teacher
PARTIAL: Student makes connection only after teacher explicitly prompts
Transfer present but teacher-prompted with 'where else have you seen this?'
Teacher invitation for connection exists but not all students take it up
NO: No connection-making activity present in lesson at all
No transfer prompts and no student-initiated connections
Students do not connect concept to life or other contexts

SLGP-4.aiDetectionMethod: Identify teacher prompts for connection-making ('where else', 'does this remind you', 'like in...'). Extract student responses that reference outside context. Verify if connection is student-initiated or teacher-prompted. Track transfer instances.

SLGP-5.name: Visible Learning Progression Across the Lesson
SLGP-5.description: Do student responses about the concept sound more complete and accurate by the end of the lesson than at the beginning?

YES: By end of lesson, students use concept's key vocabulary noticeably more often
Student responses longer and more complete than at lesson start
Clear shift in student language quality from start to end of lesson
PARTIAL: Student responses somewhat more complete by lesson end
Improvement is modest or inconsistent
Some shift in language quality but not strong or consistent
NO: Student responses look similar at end as at start
No noticeable change in vocabulary or response quality
Too few student responses to compare beginning and end

SLGP-5.aiDetectionMethod: Extract student responses about the concept from beginning, middle, and end of lesson. Analyze vocabulary richness and response length at each phase. Compare key vocabulary frequency over lesson timeline. Detect quality improvement trajectory.
